cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Science is a way of asking questions about the world, observing carefully, testing ideas and using evidence to explain what happens.
cards.note: NCERT describes this opening chapter as an introductory, non-evaluative chapter; use it to build curiosity rather than memorise it for a test.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Notice something around you, ask a testable question, make a prediction and plan a fair observation or investigation.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What makes an explanation scientific?
cards.answer: It is based on observations or evidence and can be checked through investigation.

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Living things show great diversity in their shapes, sizes, habitats and ways of life. Grouping organisms by shared features helps us study them.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Observe visible features such as body covering, movement, habitat and leaf or stem form. Group by a clear feature and explain your choice.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why do scientists group living organisms?
cards.answer: Grouping makes the huge variety of organisms easier to study and helps us recognise similarities and differences.

chapters.title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
chapters.subtitle: Curiosity · quick recall and observation

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Food provides nutrients and energy. A balanced diet includes different food groups in suitable amounts, along with safe food and healthy eating habits.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Choose a variety of foods, drink clean water and pay attention to hygiene, freshness and how food is stored.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is eating a variety of foods better than depending on only one food?
cards.answer: Different foods provide different nutrients; variety helps the body get what it needs for growth, energy and health.

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Magnets attract some materials, especially iron-containing materials. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole; like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Test materials one at a time and record the result. A freely suspended magnet settles approximately in the north–south direction.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another?
cards.answer: They attract because unlike magnetic poles attract.

chapters.title: Measurement of Length and Motion
chapters.subtitle: Units, careful measurement and types of motion

cards.title: Length and its standard unit
cards.content: Length tells us how far apart two points are. The standard SI unit of length is the metre (m). Smaller lengths are commonly measured in centimetres (cm) or millimetres (mm).

cards.title: How to measure length correctly
cards.content: Follow these steps when using a ruler or metre scale:
steps: Place the scale along the object, with the zero mark at one end.
Keep the scale parallel to the length being measured.
Look vertically above the other end and note the reading.
If the zero mark is damaged, start from another clear mark and subtract the starting reading from the final reading.
cards.note: Write the number together with its unit.

cards.title: Avoid parallax error
cards.content: Your eye should be directly above the mark being read. Looking from an angle can make the reading appear different. This is called parallax error.
cards.examTip: Keep your line of sight perpendicular to the scale at the point you are reading.

cards.title: Different kinds of motion

left.heading: Rectilinear motion
left.content: Movement along a straight line. Example: a car moving along a straight road.

right.heading: Circular motion
right.content: Movement along a circular path. Example: the tip of a fan blade while the fan rotates.

cards.note: The path followed by an object helps us describe its motion.

cards.title: Periodic motion
cards.content: A motion that repeats itself after equal intervals of time is called periodic motion.
cards.highlight: Example: the to-and-fro motion of a swing.

cards.title: Quick unit conversions
cards.note: Convert to the same unit before comparing or adding lengths.

cards.title: Check your recall
cards.question: A student reads a ruler while looking at the mark from a slanting angle. What error may occur, and how can it be avoided?
cards.answer: Parallax error may occur. Keep the eye directly above the mark and look perpendicular to the scale.

cards.title: Classify the motion
cards.question: A point on the edge of a rotating bicycle wheel follows what kind of path?
cards.answer: A circular path, so it shows circular motion.

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Objects are made from materials with different properties such as hardness, flexibility, transparency, solubility and ability to float or sink.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Choose a material for a purpose by matching its properties to the job. One material may be useful for one purpose but unsuitable for another.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is glass useful for a window but not usually for a school bag?
cards.answer: Glass is transparent and rigid but brittle; a bag needs a flexible, strong material that can withstand handling.

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is. A thermometer measures temperature; the Celsius scale is commonly used in everyday settings.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Use a suitable thermometer, read it at eye level and follow safety instructions. Do not use touch alone to judge exact temperature.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is the usual unit used to report everyday temperature in the Celsius scale?
cards.answer: Degree Celsius (°C).

chapters.title: A Journey through States of Water
chapters.subtitle: Curiosity · quick recall and observation

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Water exists as solid ice, liquid water and water vapour. Heating and cooling cause changes of state such as melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Evaporation can happen below the boiling point and is faster with more heat, moving air and a larger exposed surface.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What change of state occurs when water vapour cools and forms tiny liquid droplets?
cards.answer: Condensation.

chapters.title: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
chapters.subtitle: Curiosity · quick recall and observation

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Mixtures contain two or more substances that can often be separated using differences in size, solubility, magnetism or settling behaviour.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Choose a method based on the property that differs: sieving for particle size, filtration for insoluble solids, evaporation for dissolved solids and magnetic separation for magnetic materials.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How would you separate sand from water?
cards.answer: Use filtration: the sand remains on the filter while water passes through.

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Living organisms carry out life processes such as nutrition, growth, response to surroundings and reproduction. A single feature alone may not always identify life.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Compare several characteristics and observe an organism over time. Movement by itself does not prove that something is living.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is a moving toy not considered a living organism?
cards.answer: It does not carry out life processes such as nutrition, growth, respiration and reproduction; its movement is produced mechanically.

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Air, water, soil, rocks, minerals and living organisms are natural resources. They support life and must be used carefully so that they remain available.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Reduce waste, reuse materials, save water and energy, and protect local habitats. Notice how natural resources are connected.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why should we avoid wasting fresh water?
cards.answer: Usable fresh water is limited and is essential for people, plants and animals; careful use helps protect supplies for the future.

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Earth is part of the Solar System. The Sun is a star; planets orbit it, while the Moon is Earth's natural satellite. Stars appear as points of light because they are very far away.

cards.title: Try and apply
cards.content: Use a simple model or sky observation to distinguish a star, a planet and a natural satellite. Remember that the apparent daily motion of the sky is mainly due to Earth's rotation.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why does the Sun look much larger and brighter than other stars?
cards.answer: The Sun is a star much closer to Earth than the other stars, so it appears larger and brighter.

chapters.title: Real Numbers
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Use prime factorisation to understand HCF and LCM. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every composite integer has a unique prime factorisation, apart from order.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: For two positive integers, HCF × LCM = product of the numbers. Use prime exponents carefully.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How does prime factorisation help find the HCF and LCM of two numbers?
cards.answer: Write each number as a product of primes. For the HCF take the smallest common powers; for the LCM take the greatest powers of every prime present.

chapters.title: Polynomials
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: A polynomial is an algebraic expression in which the powers of the variable are non-negative integers. Its zeroes are the values that make it equal to zero.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: For ax² + bx + c, sum of zeroes = −b/a and product = c/a.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: For a quadratic polynomial ax² + bx + c, what do the sum and product of its zeroes equal?
cards.answer: Sum = −b/a and product = c/a, where a is non-zero.

chapters.title: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: A pair of linear equations represents two straight lines. Their intersection gives the common solution; parallel or coincident lines explain the other cases.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: For a₁x+b₁y+c₁=0 and a₂x+b₂y+c₂=0, compare coefficient ratios to identify unique, no or infinitely many solutions.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What do the coefficient ratios tell you about a pair of linear equations?
cards.answer: For a₁x+b₁y+c₁=0 and a₂x+b₂y+c₂=0: a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ gives a unique solution; if a₁/a₂=b₁/b₂≠c₁/c₂ there is no solution; if all three ratios are equal there are infinitely many solutions.

chapters.title: Quadratic Equations
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: A quadratic equation has the form ax²+bx+c=0, where a≠0. Its roots can be found by factorisation, completing the square or the quadratic formula.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: The discriminant D=b²−4ac determines the nature of roots: positive, zero or negative.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How does the discriminant predict the roots of ax²+bx+c=0?
cards.answer: For D=b²−4ac: D>0 gives two distinct real roots, D=0 gives equal real roots, and D<0 gives no real roots.

chapters.title: Arithmetic Progressions
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: An arithmetic progression has a constant common difference between consecutive terms. The nth term and sum depend on the first term and common difference.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Check the common difference before applying formulas; the sum formula uses the number of terms, not the final term.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is the nth term of an AP, and what does d represent?
cards.answer: aₙ=a+(n−1)d; a is the first term and d is the common difference.

chapters.title: Triangles
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Similarity means corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are proportional. Similar triangles have the same shape but may differ in size.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Use AA, SAS or SSS similarity criteria. In a right triangle, the Pythagoras theorem links the hypotenuse to the other two sides.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: State the Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales theorem) for a triangle.
cards.answer: A line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio.

chapters.title: Coordinate Geometry
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Coordinate geometry connects algebra and geometry using ordered pairs. Distance, section and area formulas help describe points and figures on the plane.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Keep x-coordinates with x and y-coordinates with y; use brackets carefully when subtracting negative values.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How do you find the distance between (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂)?
cards.answer: Use √[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²]. Keep the coordinate differences inside brackets, especially when negatives occur.

chapters.title: Introduction to Trigonometry
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Trigonometric ratios relate an acute angle in a right triangle to its sides: sine, cosine and tangent, with reciprocal ratios cosec, sec and cot.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Memorise opposite/hypotenuse, adjacent/hypotenuse and opposite/adjacent relative to the chosen angle.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: In a right triangle, what are sin θ, cos θ and tan θ?
cards.answer: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse; cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse; tan θ = opposite/adjacent.

chapters.title: Some Applications of Trigonometry
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Heights and distances problems use angles of elevation and depression with right-triangle trigonometry.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Draw and label a right triangle first. Decide which side is opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse before selecting a ratio.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is the difference between an angle of elevation and an angle of depression?
cards.answer: Elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; depression is measured downward from the horizontal to an object.

chapters.title: Circles
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point. The radius drawn to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Tangents from an external point to a circle are equal in length. Distinguish a tangent from a secant.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is the relationship between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact?
cards.answer: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact. Tangents from the same external point are equal in length.

chapters.title: Areas Related to Circles
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Sector and segment areas are fractions of the full circle based on the central angle. Arc length is the corresponding fraction of circumference.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Check whether the question asks for a sector, segment, ring or shaded region; subtract areas only after identifying the required shape.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How is the area of a sector with central angle θ calculated (θ in degrees)?
cards.answer: Sector area = (θ/360°) × πr². The corresponding arc length is (θ/360°) × 2πr.

chapters.title: Surface Areas and Volumes
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Mensuration combines surface area and volume formulas for solids such as cylinders, cones, spheres and combinations of solids.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Convert all measurements to the same unit. For a combined solid, add or subtract only the surfaces that are actually exposed.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is the volume of a cone, and how does it compare with a cylinder of the same base and height?
cards.answer: Cone volume = (1/3)πr²h; it is one-third of the volume of a cylinder with the same base radius and height.

chapters.title: Statistics
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Grouped data can be summarised using mean, median and mode. The median depends on cumulative frequency and the median class.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: For grouped median, identify N/2, locate the median class and substitute its lower boundary, cumulative frequency, frequency and class width correctly.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Which quantities are needed in the grouped-data median formula?
cards.answer: Median = l + [(N/2 − cf)/f] × h, where l is the lower boundary of the median class, cf the cumulative frequency before it, f its frequency and h the class width.

chapters.title: Probability
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: For equally likely outcomes, probability is favourable outcomes divided by total possible outcomes. Probability lies between 0 and 1.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Count distinct equally likely outcomes and avoid counting the same outcome twice.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is the probability of an event, and what are its limits?
cards.answer: For equally likely outcomes, P(E)=number of favourable outcomes/total outcomes; 0≤P(E)≤1.

chapters.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms to form new substances. A balanced equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides, obeying conservation of mass.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Identify the reaction type—combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement or redox—and balance by changing coefficients, never subscripts.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
cards.answer: It must show the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, reflecting conservation of mass. Change coefficients, never subscripts, when balancing.

chapters.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Acids produce H⁺/H₃O⁺ ions in aqueous solution; bases produce OH⁻ ions. Neutralisation forms salt and water.
cards.highlight: pH < 7 acid; pH = 7 neutral; pH > 7 base

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Use indicators and pH to compare solutions. Strong/weak describes ionisation; concentrated/dilute describes amount per volume.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What does the pH scale indicate, and how do acids and bases compare?
cards.answer: pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is basic. In aqueous solution acids furnish H⁺/H₃O⁺ ions and bases furnish OH⁻ ions.

chapters.title: Metals and Non-metals
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Metals generally lose electrons to form cations; non-metals generally gain or share electrons. Reactivity determines displacement and extraction methods.
cards.highlight: More reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Remember that reactivity series predicts displacement. Ionic compounds conduct when molten or dissolved, not as solids.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why can ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved but not as solids?
cards.answer: In solids, ions are fixed in a lattice. When molten or dissolved, ions are free to move and carry electric charge.

chapters.title: Carbon and its Compounds
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Carbon forms covalent bonds and long chains because of tetravalency and catenation. Saturated compounds have single bonds; unsaturated compounds contain double or triple bonds.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Know homologous series, functional groups, combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions; draw structural formulas clearly.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What are catenation and tetravalency, and why are they important for carbon?
cards.answer: Catenation is carbon's ability to bond with itself to form chains/rings; tetravalency means it forms four covalent bonds. Together they allow a huge variety of compounds.

chapters.title: Periodic Classification of Elements
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: The modern periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number. Elements in a group share valence-electron patterns; periods indicate occupied shells.
cards.note: 2026–27 CBSE scope: formative/portfolio only; not assessed in the year-end examination.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Across a period, atomic size generally decreases and metallic character decreases; down a group, atomic size generally increases.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What determines an element's position in the modern periodic table?
cards.answer: Increasing atomic number determines the order. Elements in a group have similar valence-electron configurations and often similar chemical properties.

chapters.title: Life Processes
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Living organisms maintain themselves through nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion. These processes exchange matter and energy with the environment.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Trace the pathway, organ and function for each process; compare autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition and aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Name the four basic life processes that maintain an organism.
cards.answer: Nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion.

chapters.title: Control and Coordination
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Nervous and hormonal systems coordinate responses. Neurons transmit impulses; hormones act as chemical messengers through target organs.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Reflex actions are rapid and often involve the spinal cord. Plant hormones coordinate growth and tropic responses.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How does a reflex action differ from a voluntary action?
cards.answer: A reflex is a rapid, automatic response often coordinated through the spinal cord; a voluntary action is consciously initiated and controlled by the brain.

chapters.title: How do Organisms Reproduce?
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Reproduction produces new individuals. Asexual reproduction uses one parent; sexual reproduction involves gametes and fertilisation, generating variation.
cards.highlight: Gametes fuse to form a zygote

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Distinguish pollination from fertilisation in plants and identify the roles of testes, ovaries, uterus and placenta in humans.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is the key difference between asexual and sexual reproduction?
cards.answer: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no fusion of gametes; sexual reproduction involves male and female gametes and fertilisation.

chapters.title: Heredity (Evolution – formative enrichment)
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Heredity is the transmission of traits from parents to offspring through genes. Mendel's experiments explain inheritance patterns, including dominant and recessive traits; sex determination is also introduced.
cards.note: Evolution topics in the 2026–27 reading material are formative enrichment and are not assessed in the year-end examination.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Focus on Mendel's contribution, laws/patterns of inheritance and the brief introduction to sex determination. Treat evolution subtopics as formative enrichment.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What did Mendel's experiments establish about inheritance?
cards.answer: Traits are passed through discrete factors (now called genes); alternative forms can show dominant and recessive patterns. The 2026–27 year-end focus is heredity; evolution topics are formative enrichment.

chapters.title: Light: Reflection and Refraction
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Reflection changes the direction of light at a surface; refraction occurs when light changes speed between media. Spherical mirrors and lenses form images.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Use the correct sign convention and draw principal rays. Distinguish real/inverted from virtual/erect images.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: State the mirror formula and the lens formula used in Class 10 ray optics.
cards.answer: Using the Cartesian sign convention: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u for spherical mirrors and thin lenses. Apply the correct sign to u, v and f.

chapters.title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: The eye focuses light on the retina. Accommodation changes lens curvature; scattering and refraction explain several atmospheric optical effects.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Myopia is corrected with a concave lens; hypermetropia with a convex lens. Know dispersion, scattering and the blue appearance of the sky.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Which lenses correct myopia and hypermetropia?
cards.answer: Myopia (distant objects appear blurred) is corrected by a concave lens; hypermetropia (near objects appear blurred) is corrected by a convex lens.

chapters.title: Electricity
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge. Potential difference drives current; resistance opposes it. Series and parallel combinations behave differently.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Use V=IR and P=VI. In series, current is common; in parallel, potential difference is common.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How are current, potential difference and resistance related?
cards.answer: Ohm's law: V=IR. Current is charge per unit time; potential difference is work per unit charge; resistance is the opposition to current.

chapters.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field. Motors convert electrical energy to mechanical energy; electromagnetic induction produces current from changing magnetic flux.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Revise magnetic fields around conductors and solenoids, force on a current-carrying conductor, Fleming's left-hand rule, direct and alternating current, frequency and domestic circuits.
cards.note: Motor, electromagnetic induction and electric generator are formative-only topics in the 2026–27 year-end scope.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Which rule gives the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field?
cards.answer: Fleming's left-hand rule. The thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand are held mutually perpendicular for force, field and current respectively.

chapters.title: Our Environment
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Ecosystems contain producers, consumers and decomposers. Energy flows through trophic levels while materials are recycled.
cards.highlight: Energy flow is one-way; nutrients cycle

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Only a small fraction of energy passes to the next trophic level; biomagnification increases concentration of persistent pollutants up food chains.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why does energy decrease at successive trophic levels?
cards.answer: Only a small fraction (about 10%) of energy is transferred to the next trophic level; most is used in life processes or lost as heat.

chapters.title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: The French Revolution popularised citizenship and the nation as a source of sovereignty. Liberalism, cultural movements and political struggles shaped nineteenth-century nationalism.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Connect unification of Germany and Italy with key leaders, events and the role of conservative powers; distinguish nation-state from empire.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What did the French Revolution contribute to the growth of nationalism in Europe?
cards.answer: It promoted ideas of citizenship, popular sovereignty and the nation as a community of citizens, challenging dynastic rule and privilege.

chapters.title: Nationalism in India
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Indian nationalism grew through anti-colonial movements, mass mobilisation and shared symbols. Gandhi linked local grievances to broader satyagraha campaigns.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Keep the sequence clear: Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation, then Civil Disobedience and the Salt March. Track how different groups participated and where their aims differed.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Which major movements followed the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh, and what was the key later mass campaign?
cards.answer: The Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements followed; later Gandhi launched the Civil Disobedience Movement with the Salt March. Do not confuse this chapter's timeline with the 1942 Quit India Movement.

chapters.title: The Making of a Global World
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: The board-exam portion covers the pre-modern world: long-distance trade routes, the movement of food and crops, and how conquest, disease and trade connected and transformed societies.

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Revise the Silk Routes, food travels (such as potatoes and other crops), and the effects of conquest, disease and trade. Later sections are for the interdisciplinary project, not the board theory paper.
cards.note: Project-only scope: subtopics 2–4.4 (nineteenth century to post-war globalisation).

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: For the board-exam portion (subtopics 1–1.3), name two examples of pre-modern global connections.
cards.answer: The Silk Routes linked regions through trade and cultural exchange; food crops travelled across continents, while conquest, disease and trade reshaped societies.

chapters.title: Print Culture and the Modern World
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Printing transformed the circulation of ideas, literacy, religious debate and political discussion. Print culture developed differently across societies.
cards.highlight: Print expanded access to ideas and debate

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Explain how print affected reform, public debate and nationalism; distinguish manuscript culture from mass print.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How did print culture change the circulation of ideas?
cards.answer: Printing made texts more reproducible and accessible, expanded reading publics and stimulated religious reform, debate and political discussion.

chapters.title: Resources and Development
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Resources become useful through technology, institutions and human effort. Sustainable development balances present needs with future generations.
cards.highlight: Sustainable use = present needs + future capacity

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Classify resources by origin, exhaustibility, ownership and status; connect resource planning with conservation and land degradation.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is resource planning important in India?
cards.answer: Resources are unevenly distributed and can be depleted or degraded. Planning helps match technology, institutions and skills to judicious, sustainable use.

chapters.title: Forest and Wildlife Resources
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Biodiversity supports ecological balance and livelihoods. Habitat loss, hunting and development pressures threaten species and forest ecosystems.
cards.highlight: In-situ conservation protects species in natural habitats

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Know conservation categories and community-led examples; distinguish endangered, vulnerable and endemic species.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is biodiversity conservation important?
cards.answer: Biodiversity maintains ecological balance and supports livelihoods; conservation protects habitats, species and ecosystem services for future generations.

chapters.title: Water Resources
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Freshwater is limited and unevenly distributed. Multipurpose river projects support irrigation and power but can also cause social and ecological impacts.
cards.highlight: Rainwater harvesting improves local water security

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Compare dams’ benefits and costs; explain rainwater harvesting and watershed management with local examples.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Give one benefit and one concern associated with multipurpose river projects.
cards.answer: They can provide irrigation, hydroelectricity and flood control; they can also displace communities and disrupt river ecosystems.

chapters.title: Agriculture
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Agriculture depends on climate, soil, technology, labour and markets. Cropping seasons and farming types vary across India.
cards.highlight: Kharif: monsoon · Rabi: winter · Zaid: short summer

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Compare Kharif, Rabi and Zaid crops; link crop requirements to temperature, rainfall and soil.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How do Kharif and Rabi cropping seasons differ?
cards.answer: Kharif crops are generally sown with the monsoon and harvested in autumn; Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in spring.

chapters.title: Minerals and Energy Resources
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Minerals occur in different geological formations and are essential for industry. Energy resources are renewable or non-renewable.
cards.highlight: Conservation reduces depletion and environmental cost

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Connect mineral type to mode of occurrence and conservation; distinguish conventional and non-conventional energy sources.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why should minerals and energy resources be used carefully?
cards.answer: Many are finite and take geological time to form; conservation, efficient use and suitable renewable alternatives support long-term development.

chapters.title: Manufacturing Industries
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Manufacturing adds value to raw materials and supports employment, trade and economic development. Industrial location depends on several factors.
cards.highlight: Industry location: raw material + power + labour + market + transport

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Explain agglomeration, industrial pollution and control measures; use examples of major industries and their location factors.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Name two major factors that influence the location of an industry.
cards.answer: Access to raw materials, power, labour, capital, transport, markets and supporting infrastructure influence industrial location.

chapters.title: Power Sharing
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Power sharing reduces conflict and strengthens democracy by distributing authority among organs, levels and social groups.
cards.highlight: Power sharing is both prudent and morally desirable

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Compare Belgium’s accommodation with Sri Lanka’s majoritarian policies; identify horizontal and vertical power sharing.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is power sharing desirable in a democracy?
cards.answer: It reduces the possibility of social conflict and ensures political stability; it is also valuable because people have a right to be consulted in how they are governed.

chapters.title: Federalism
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Federalism divides power between levels of government, with constitutionally protected jurisdictions. India combines a strong Union with state and local governments.
cards.highlight: Union List · State List · Concurrent List

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Remember the three lists and the role of decentralisation, linguistic states and local self-government.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What makes a government system federal?
cards.answer: Power is constitutionally divided between at least two levels of government, and each level has its own jurisdiction that the other cannot unilaterally change.

chapters.title: Gender, Religion and Caste
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Social divisions shape political life. Democracy requires equal citizenship and safeguards against discrimination and domination.
cards.highlight: Secular state: no official religion; equal treatment

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Distinguish gender division, communalism and caste inequality; explain when social differences enrich or threaten democracy.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: When can social differences become a threat to democracy?
cards.answer: When they are used to create hierarchy, exclusion or domination; democratic politics should protect equal citizenship and allow differences to be expressed without discrimination.

chapters.title: Political Parties
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Political parties contest elections, form governments, shape policies and connect citizens with institutions. They are essential to representative democracy.
cards.highlight: Parties organise political competition and accountability

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Know party functions, challenges such as dynastic succession and money power, and reforms to improve internal democracy.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: State three important functions of political parties.
cards.answer: They contest elections, form and run governments, and shape public policy; they also represent interests and connect citizens with institutions.

chapters.title: Outcomes of Democracy
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Democracy is evaluated through accountable government, responsive decision-making, legitimacy, economic outcomes and social equality.
cards.highlight: Democracy promises accountability, not instant perfection

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Avoid claiming democracy automatically removes inequality; assess outcomes using evidence and multiple dimensions.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Name two ways to assess the outcomes of democracy.
cards.answer: Assess whether government is accountable, responsive and legitimate, and whether democracy protects equality, dignity and freedom; economic equality is not automatic.

chapters.title: Development
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Development has different goals for different people. Income matters, but health, education, security, freedom and sustainability also matter.
cards.highlight: Per capita income = total income ÷ population

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Compare per capita income with human development indicators; understand public facilities and sustainable development.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is per capita income not enough to measure development?
cards.answer: It is an average and hides inequality; health, education, security, freedom, public facilities and sustainability also matter.

chapters.title: Sectors of the Indian Economy
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Economic activities are grouped into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors. Employment and output shares can differ across sectors.
cards.highlight: Primary → natural resources; Secondary → manufacturing; Tertiary → services

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Distinguish organised/unorganised and public/private sectors; explain underemployment and the role of MGNREGA.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How are the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors distinguished?
cards.answer: Primary activities obtain natural products; secondary activities manufacture or process them; tertiary activities provide services.

chapters.title: Money and Credit
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Money acts as a medium of exchange and removes the need for double coincidence of wants. Credit can support activity but may create debt traps.
cards.highlight: Formal credit is regulated; informal credit often costs more

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Compare formal and informal credit; explain collateral, terms of credit, SHGs and the role of the RBI.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How does money solve the problem of double coincidence of wants?
cards.answer: Money acts as a commonly accepted medium of exchange, so each person can sell and buy without needing to find someone who wants exactly what they offer.

chapters.title: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
chapters.subtitle: Quick recall · key ideas · exam focus

cards.title: Core idea
cards.content: Globalisation is the growing integration of economies through cross-border trade and investment, supported by technology and policy changes.
cards.highlight: Board exam scope: What is globalisation?

cards.title: Exam focus
cards.content: Explain globalisation and the factors that enabled it, especially improvements in technology and liberalisation of trade and investment. Production across countries, WTO and fair globalisation are interdisciplinary-project topics.
cards.note: Project topics are not part of the listed board-theory subtopics.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is globalisation, and name two factors that have enabled it?
cards.answer: Globalisation is the integration of production and markets across countries. Improved technology and liberalisation of trade and investment policies have enabled it.

chapters.title: Lifelines of National Economy (Map Work)
chapters.subtitle: Map identification and location practice · map-only board assessment

cards.title: What to locate
cards.content: For the 2026–27 board examination, this Geography chapter is assessed through map pointing only. Practise identifying major sea ports and international airports as listed in the official map-work syllabus.
cards.highlight: Map work only · no theory chapter assessment

cards.title: Map-work checklist
facts: Major sea ports and international airports
Locate, label and identify each prescribed point on an outline map
cards.note: Use the exact current CBSE map-work list supplied by the school.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How is Lifelines of National Economy assessed in the 2026–27 board examination?
cards.answer: Only map pointing is assessed. Practise the prescribed major sea ports and international airports; check the current CBSE map-work list for the exact locations.

chapters.title: The Age of Industrialisation
chapters.subtitle: Periodic-assessment revision · not part of the board theory paper

cards.title: Industrialisation and production
cards.content: Industrialisation transformed production through factories, machinery, new sources of power and changing systems of labour. Its effects differed between Britain and colonial India.
cards.note: CBSE 2026–27: this chapter is assessed as part of Periodic Assessment only, not the board theory examination.

cards.title: Key contrasts to revise
cards.content: Compare hand production and factory production; explain the role of merchants, workers and machines; trace how industrialisation affected Indian weavers and markets.
cards.note: Use this for school periodic assessments and class revision.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How did the rise of factories change production and work?
cards.answer: Factories brought workers and machines together under one system, increased large-scale production and changed labour conditions and markets. The effects varied by region and industry.

cards.title: Faith, hope and irony
cards.content: Lencho’s faith is sincere, but the ending uses irony to show how unquestioning belief can lead to an unexpected misunderstanding.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Explain how the post office employees respond compassionately while Lencho misreads their help.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is the ending ironic?
cards.answer: Lencho calls the helpers a ‘bunch of crooks’ even though they collected money for him; the reader knows they were his benefactors.

chapters.title: Nelson Mandela – Long Walk to Freedom
chapters.subtitle: First Flight · Prose

cards.title: Freedom and shared responsibility
cards.content: Mandela presents freedom as indivisible: personal liberty is tied to the dignity and freedom of others. Courage is acting despite fear.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Connect apartheid, sacrifice, courage and the idea that both the oppressed and oppressor are deprived of humanity.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How does Mandela redefine courage?
cards.answer: Courage is not the absence of fear; it is triumph over fear.

cards.title: Fear overcome through action
cards.content: The two narratives show how fear can be overcome through trust, determination and a willingness to act in uncertain situations.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Contrast the young seagull’s hunger-driven first flight with the pilot’s mysterious experience in the storm.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What finally makes the young seagull fly?
cards.answer: Hunger and the mother’s carefully placed food push him to leap; he discovers his wings can support him.

chapters.title: From the Diary of Anne Frank
chapters.subtitle: First Flight · Prose

cards.title: Adolescence and self-expression
cards.content: Anne uses her diary as a trusted confidante and reflects on loneliness, school life, identity and the need to express thoughts honestly.
cards.highlight: A diary can become a trusted friend

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Remember why Anne names her diary Kitty and how humour and self-awareness shape her voice.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why does Anne feel the need to write a diary?
cards.answer: She has family and friends but feels she lacks a true confidante with whom she can share her innermost thoughts.

cards.title: Cultural diversity and local traditions
cards.content: The three accounts celebrate regional identity through Goa’s baker, Coorg’s landscape and people, and Assam’s tea culture.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Use one distinctive detail from each account to show how food, landscape, work and tradition shape place identity.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What links the three accounts?
cards.answer: Each presents a distinctive Indian region through its people, traditions, landscape and everyday culture.

cards.title: Human–animal companionship
cards.content: The narrative follows the author’s growing bond with Mijbil, showing curiosity, playfulness and the challenges of caring for an unusual pet.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Recall Mijbil’s playful habits and the practical difficulties of travelling with him.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How does Mijbil show his playful nature?
cards.answer: Through inventive games with water, objects and small rolling items, revealing curiosity and intelligence.

cards.title: Childhood curiosity and independence
cards.content: Valli plans a bus journey with careful observation and saving. The ride brings excitement but also a first encounter with death.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Contrast Valli’s confidence during the ride with her quietness after seeing the dead cow.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What changes Valli’s mood on the return journey?
cards.answer: The sight of the cow she had earlier seen alive lying dead on the roadside makes her confront mortality.

cards.title: Impermanence and overcoming grief
cards.content: Kisa Gotami learns that death is universal. The Buddha guides her from personal grief toward acceptance of the impermanent nature of life.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Explain the mustard-seed task and why it changes Kisa Gotami’s understanding.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why can Kisa Gotami not find a house untouched by death?
cards.answer: Every family has experienced loss; she realises that death is universal, not a private misfortune.

cards.title: Comedy, pride and social satire
cards.content: The one-act play uses quarrels over land and dogs to mock vanity, materialism and the absurdity of social behaviour.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Track how the argument shifts from Oxen Meadows to the dogs; note the stage directions and exaggerated reactions.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is the play called a farce?
cards.answer: The characters repeatedly turn a marriage proposal into ridiculous arguments over trivial matters.

cards.title: Small moments can transform mood
cards.content: A brief encounter with nature—a crow shaking snow from a hemlock tree—changes the speaker’s gloomy mood and saves part of the day.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Notice the contrast between traditionally negative symbols and the positive emotional change.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is the effect of the dust of snow?
cards.answer: It lifts the speaker’s mood and makes the day feel less wasted.

cards.title: Destructive human emotions
cards.content: Fire symbolises desire and ice symbolises hatred. The poem warns that either extreme can destroy the world.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Explain the symbolism rather than treating fire and ice only as physical elements.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What do fire and ice represent?
cards.answer: Fire represents uncontrolled desire; ice represents hatred or cold indifference.

cards.title: Freedom versus captivity
cards.content: The caged tiger’s suppressed power contrasts with the freedom it should have in the forest, exposing the cruelty of confinement.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Contrast the tiger’s imagined movement in the jungle with its silent pacing in the cage.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is the central contrast?
cards.answer: The tiger’s natural strength and freedom are reduced to helpless confinement in the zoo.

cards.title: Humour through exaggeration
cards.content: The poem uses mock instructions, wordplay and exaggerated danger to create comic descriptions of wild animals.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Identify how the poet turns dangerous encounters into absurd identification tests.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How does the poem create humour?
cards.answer: By presenting obviously dangerous encounters as if they were simple ways to identify animals.

cards.title: Loss and emotional maturity
cards.content: A boy’s lost ball becomes a lesson in accepting loss and understanding that some experiences cannot be replaced by money.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Explain why the poet does not simply offer another ball.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What does the ball symbolise?
cards.answer: It represents a personal loss that teaches the boy responsibility and emotional maturity.

cards.title: Childhood freedom and constant instruction
cards.content: The poem contrasts an adult’s repeated commands with Amanda’s imagined worlds, highlighting the child’s desire for space and independence.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Identify the contrast between the speaker’s instructions and Amanda’s daydreams.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why does Amanda imagine being a mermaid or an orphan?
cards.answer: Her fantasies offer escape from constant correction and a desire for freedom.

cards.title: Nature’s movement toward freedom
cards.content: Trees moving out of a house symbolise nature reclaiming its place and breaking artificial confinement.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Read the movement from indoor stillness to outdoor release as a symbolic process.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What do the trees symbolise?
cards.answer: They symbolise nature’s urge for freedom from human-imposed confinement.

cards.title: Nature captured in a brief image
cards.content: The fog is compared to a cat that arrives silently, sits observing and moves away without announcement.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Notice how the cat image conveys silence, softness and temporary presence.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is fog compared to a cat?
cards.answer: Both arrive quietly, pause, observe and depart silently.

chapters.title: The Tale of Custard the Dragon
chapters.subtitle: First Flight · Poem

cards.title: Real courage versus appearance
cards.content: Custard is mocked as timid, but he alone confronts the pirate when danger arrives. The poem questions superficial ideas of bravery.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Contrast boastful claims with what each character actually does during the attack.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Who proves truly brave?
cards.answer: Custard, because he faces the pirate while the others flee.

cards.title: Inner beauty and love
cards.content: The poem questions whether human love can look beyond physical appearance and suggests that divine love alone is free from outward attraction.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Explain the contrast between golden hair and the person beneath it.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What question does the poem raise?
cards.answer: Whether people love a person for inner qualities or are influenced by outward appearance.

cards.title: Overindulgence and responsible care
cards.content: Tricki’s illness is caused by overfeeding and lack of exercise. The veterinary surgeon restores health through routine, activity and controlled diet.
cards.highlight: Care is not the same as indulgence

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Explain Mrs Pumphrey’s role and the simple treatment that helps Tricki recover.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What actually cures Tricki?
cards.answer: A balanced routine, exercise and controlled food—not elaborate medicines.

cards.title: Trust can reform
cards.content: Anil’s trust and generosity create the conditions for Hari Singh to return the stolen money and choose education over theft.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Explain the significance of the damp notes and Anil’s quiet response.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why does Hari return?
cards.answer: He values Anil’s trust and the opportunity to learn, and begins to choose an honest future.

cards.title: Presence of mind beats appearance
cards.content: Ausable defeats Max through calm improvisation, using a fictional balcony and a knock at the door to escape danger.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Track how Ausable invents details and uses Fowler’s and Max’s assumptions against Max.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How does Ausable outwit Max?
cards.answer: He invents a balcony and pretends the approaching waiter is the police, prompting Max to jump out.

cards.title: Overconfidence invites deception
cards.content: Horace Danby is a careful thief, yet he is tricked by a woman posing as the house owner and is caught because he trusts appearances.
cards.highlight: A thief can also be deceived

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Explain the irony of Horace’s expertise and the woman’s deception.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why is Horace arrested?
cards.answer: He leaves fingerprints while opening the safe for the woman who has deceived him.

cards.title: Science without ethics is dangerous
cards.content: Griffin’s invisibility gives him power, but his selfishness and lawlessness turn scientific discovery into a threat.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Connect Griffin’s scientific achievement with his antisocial actions.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is Griffin’s main flaw?
cards.answer: He uses scientific discovery for selfish and criminal purposes rather than responsible benefit.

cards.title: Curiosity and persistence create achievement
cards.content: Richard Ebright’s scientific success grows from curiosity, careful observation, experimentation, reading and guidance.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Remember the role of his mother, butterfly collection and step-by-step scientific investigations.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What qualities help Ebright succeed?
cards.answer: Curiosity, perseverance, observation, experimentation and willingness to learn from failure.

cards.title: Vanity and consequences
cards.content: Matilda’s dissatisfaction with her life leads to a borrowed necklace, years of sacrifice and a final revelation about the necklace’s true value.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Explain the irony at the end and how one unverified assumption changes the couple’s life.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: What is the central irony?
cards.answer: The necklace was imitation jewellery, but the couple spent years repaying the cost of a replacement.

cards.title: Education builds confidence
cards.content: Bholi’s teacher gives her confidence and a voice. Her refusal to marry a greedy man shows self-respect and the power of education.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Contrast Bholi’s early stammering and fear with her final decision.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: Why does Bholi refuse the marriage?
cards.answer: She rejects Bishamber’s demand for dowry and chooses dignity over an insulting marriage.

chapters.title: The Book That Saved the Earth
chapters.subtitle: Footprints Without Feet

cards.title: Humour and misunderstanding
cards.content: A comic science-fiction play shows how a nursery rhyme book is misinterpreted by Martians, saving Earth through accidental misunderstanding.

cards.title: What to write in an answer
cards.content: Explain Think-Tank’s misreadings and how Noodle’s cautious suggestions expose faulty reasoning.
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: Quick self-check
cards.question: How does the book save Earth?
cards.answer: Martians mistake nursery rhymes for dangerous coded information and abandon their invasion.

cards.title: मुख्य विचार
cards.content: हालदार साहब की दृष्टि से कैप्टन और मूर्ति का प्रसंग छोटे नगर में जीवित देशभक्ति और सम्मान की भावना दिखाता है।
cards.highlight: देशप्रेम केवल बड़े कार्यों में नहीं, छोटे व्यवहार में भी दिखता है।

cards.title: परीक्षा में ध्यान दें
cards.content: कैप्टन की देशभक्ति और मूर्ति पर चश्मा लगाने के प्रसंग का अर्थ स्पष्ट करें।
cards.examTip: Answer the question asked; support interpretations with specific textual details, not a retelling of the whole chapter.

cards.title: त्वरित स्व-जाँच
cards.question: कहानी में चश्मा किसका प्रतीक है?
cards.answer: चश्मा नेताजी के प्रति सम्मान, देशभक्ति और आदर्शों को जीवित रखने का प्रतीक है।
